Putin lets Europe join Ukraine peace talks, Zelenskiy welcomes prospect of European participation

Reuters

13 November, 2026 05:30 am IST

By Andrew Osborn and Padraic Halpin MOSCOW/DUBLIN, Nov 12 (Reuters) – President Vladimir Putin agreed on Thursday to let European representatives join the next round of Ukraine peace talks, a US envoy said, though the Russian leader said Washington must work with its European allies to understand if they want peace or war in Ukraine.

The move to give Europe a seat at the negotiating table at the next round of talks, which US envoy Steve Witkoff announced after the talks, could mark a breakthrough. But Putin’s comments underlined how difficult the negotiations could become, given sharp differences between Moscow and European capitals over the way the war should end.

“The Europeans will join at the next meeting, which we consider to be a very important moment because they are our partners and it’s important to us that they take part,” Witkoff told Russian state TV after meeting Putin in the Kremlin.

Show Full Article

Witkoff and fellow US presidential envoy Jared Kushner later flew to Ireland and met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who said he was pleased at the prospect of further sets of talks and European participation in them.

There were, however, signs of renewed tensions, with Zelenskiy saying new restrictions were affecting the US-made satellite communications Kyiv uses on the battlefield, and that he found the US approach of discussing a new European security order with Russia “a bit strange”.

EU ROLE IN TALKS?

During the Kremlin talks, Kushner told Putin that Washington had detected what he called “a big change” on the European side and was confident that expanding peace talks to include the Europeans would not hinder progress.

Putin said Moscow had always been open to talking to the EU about Ukraine, but signalled serious outstanding differences.

“As far as the Europeans are concerned, we have never been opposed to engaging in dialogue with Europe, and we have never broken off that dialogue. It was they who broke off the dialogue with the Russian Federation,” he said.

He then warned that the European idea of sending Western troops into Ukraine once a peace deal was concluded would trigger a resumption of the war because Russia would see that as a threat to its own security.

“We would very much like you, gentlemen, and the US administration as a whole, to work with your European allies so that they can finally make up their minds as to what they want: peace or war in Ukraine,” said Putin.

In a briefing after the talks, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov did not confirm that the Europeans would join the next round of peace talks and said their current stance on Ukraine amounted to “a recipe for endless war.”

After Zelenskiy’s brief discussions with the two US envoys in Ireland, the Ukrainian president welcomed news that Europeans would be present at the next round of peace talks and expressed hope that the agenda would include steps towards a ceasefire and de-escalating the conflict.

“It’s important that everything is unblocked,” Zelenskiy said, after meeting the envoys whilst in Dublin to attend a European summit.

“We decided that we will work on an agenda about any kind of de-escalation, some kind of ceasefires… I hope that we will have such agenda. Yes, this is important.”

The two days of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi this week were the first direct US-mediated negotiations between Russia and Ukraine in nine months.

Kyiv and Moscow said there had been some progress but that major differences remained, including on territorial issues. Russia holds about one-fifth of Ukraine and Kyiv refuses to give up the rest of the Donbas region in its east.

Earlier on Thursday, Zelenskiy said disruptions to the Starshield satellite communications service were significant, affecting the entire front line and Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine. Starshield is the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications service, and Ukraine suffered similar disruptions last month.

“So far we know very little (on the Starshield restrictions). But some things are already clear: if someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then it tells us where things are going,” he said.

In a post on Telegram, he said that systemic restrictions were limiting the speed at which Starshield could be used. SpaceX declined to comment.

PROPOSED AID MISSION

In Moscow, Putin told the US envoys that Russia was proposing a joint Russian-Ukrainian humanitarian mission to Kostiantynivka in eastern Ukraine, which he said Moscow controlled, an assertion Ukraine has taken issue with in the past, saying it retains a presence there.

Putin said the mission could be modeled on an initiative that allowed residents to leave the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine at the end of last month and for aid to be brought in for those who chose to remain.

Russia needed five days to clear the area near Kostiantynivka of mines, Putin said, saying there were 400 to 500 city residents who were still there. The mission would allow the world to understand who controlled the city, he added.

Ushakov, the Kremlin aide, said the US envoys had welcomed Putin’s idea and would be in touch with Russia about it.

Kyiv has expressed concerns that Moscow might wish to use ceasefires for such missions to enable its military to regroup.

Moscow has not made major territorial gains this year, but has heavily attacked Ukrainian infrastructure and Kyiv has frequently struck Russian oil refineries with drones, causing fuel shortages over the summer, a problem which has resurfaced in some regions this week, according to local officials.

Putin has shown no signs of being ready to moderate his territorial demands, which include a buffer zone in parts of Ukraine which Russia has not formally claimed as its own. He said on Thursday that what Russia considers its state border should be the only meaningful demarcation point with Ukraine, in comments which appeared to signal his determination to pursue his aim of taking full control of all four Ukrainian regions that Moscow says it annexed in 2022.

(Reporting by Reuters; Additional reporting by Dmitry Antonov in Moscow, Maxim Rodionov in London, Daniel Flynn in Kyiv, Padraic Halpin in Dublin; Writing by Andrew Osborn; Editing by Timothy Heritage, Ron Popeski and Lincoln Feast.)

By Maria Tsvetkova NEW YORK, Nov 12 (Reuters) – Rescue teams worked through torrential rain on Thursday in search of victims still buried in the rubble of a New York City apartment building collapse that killed at least eight people and prompted Mayor Zohran Mamdani to order an investigation into dozens of linked construction sites.

A day after Wednesday’s late-afternoon collapse in the city’s Brooklyn borough, Mamdani said the city would examine five companies associated with a construction site adjacent to the collapse and 100 more sites connected with those entities.

The construction site was undergoing excavation work that started earlier this year, historical satellite imagery showed. An official notice filed by a construction company in September informed authorities that the earthwork included “rock blasting,” official records showed.

Show Full Article

Six people were found dead in the wreckage and two others died later from their injuries, city officials told reporters at the scene of the collapse. Two of those killed were children. The six adults killed included two construction workers.

Those injured in the collapse and its aftermath stood at 18, including four of the firefighters who led the rescue effort, officials said.

Municipal building inspectors fanned out across the city to conduct inspections of the other sites “to ensure that if there is anything for New Yorkers to be worried about that we are on the scene and we are doing something about it,” the mayor said at a press conference.

“If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable,” Mamdani said.

The apartment building, which Mamdani said was home to several immigrant families, was built in 1930 and consisted of four residential units, according to official records. Two Ecuadoreans were among the dead.

The building collapsed around 4 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Wednesday and destroyed a wall of an adjacent residential block, exposing a staircase, closets and a bedroom.

Three other addresses were ordered vacated on the same side of the street as a precaution until safety inspections could be conducted, officials said.

On Thursday, two excavators were seen at the construction site clearing the debris under pouring rain. Mamdani said rescue work by some 250 personnel was continuing around the clock.”We will be here until we are 100% sure there are no more people trapped,” Fire Department Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore told reporters. “We always assume that there are more people there until we can access the ground. So until we remove some of the bigger debris and are able to search beneath them, this will remain a rescue operation.”

(Reporting by Maria Tsvetkova in New York; Additional reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles and Jonathan Allen in New York; Editing by Howard Goller)

By David Brunnstrom

WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) – The leader of Tibet’s government-in-exile expressed disappointment that human rights appeared absent from US President Donald Trump’s dealings with China, telling Reuters that a focus solely on trade and business risked emboldening Beijing.

Penpa Tsering said in an interview on Wednesday night that US support for Tibet remained broadly stable under the Trump administration, but Tibet was not on the agenda at the presidential level as Washington focuses on trade, security and other priorities with China.

Show Full Article

“(Trump) has never mentioned Tibet, he has never mentioned human rights,” he said during a visit to Washington.

China seized control of Tibet in 1950 in what it describes as a “peaceful liberation” from feudalistic serfdom.

International human rights groups and exiles have routinely condemned what they call China’s oppressive rule in Tibetan areas, assessments Beijing rejects.

Tsering said the US remained the Tibetan exile movement’s most important international partner and Tibet enjoyed strong bipartisan backing in Congress.

He said his Central Tibetan Administration continued to engage with the State Department, and noted that Secretary of State Marco Rubio was a longtime champion of Tibet-related legislation when he was a senator.

While State Department foreign assistance cuts halved money for Tibet last year, Tsering expressed optimism that full funding would be restored later this year and noted that the current Trump administration appointed a special coordinator for Tibetan issues in its second year, compared with the fourth year of Trump’s first term.

TIBET UNLIKELY TO FEATURE IN TRUMP-XI TALKS

Tsering said he did not expect Tibet to feature in Trump’s planned meetings with Chinese leader Xi Jinping at next week’s APEC summit or at the G20 summit in Florida next month and suggested this may be preferable to becoming a bargaining chip in broader US-China negotiations.

“Maybe sometimes it’s better that way,” he said. “Instead of becoming a bargaining chip. And China is very good in creating leverages.”

However, he said Western governments had become overly focused on trade and economic ties with China while neglecting rights concerns, strengthening China’s power in the process.

“Knowing that the dragon is biting at you, if you still keep feeding them, then whose fault is it?” he said.

“We should be talking more on balancing trade … with human rights and other things, which is not happening so much these days, unfortunately, even people who accuse America of backsliding on democracy still suck up to China.”

He highlighted China’s “ethnic unity and progress” policies, saying they were aimed at weakening Tibetan identity, language, religion and culture. He said Chinese authorities were becoming more open about assimilation policies and faced little international pushback.

China does not recognize the exiled government and has defended its rule in Tibet as bringing much-needed development to what was a backward and feudal society.

(Reporting by David Brunnstrom; Editing by Don Durfee and Sanjeev Miglani)
